entities.name: Qatada ibn al-Nu'man
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Qatada ibn al-Nu'man (c. 581–c. 644 CE) emerged as a pivotal companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and a distinguished member of the Ansar, the indigenous Medinan converts who provided crucial support to the nascent Muslim community. His significance lies in his unwavering commitment during the formative years of Islam, particularly his participation in key military campaigns and his role as a transmitter of prophetic traditions (Hadith), thereby helping to solidify the legal and ethical framework of early Muslim society. As one of the Banu Zafar clan of the Aws tribe, Qatada's lineage positioned him within the established social fabric of Medina, lending credibility and strength to the new religious movement during its critical period of expansion and consolidation.

A veteran of nearly every major engagement from the Battle of Badr in 624 CE to the conquest of Mecca in 630 CE, Qatada ibn al-Nu'man distinguished himself through his courage and loyalty. Notably, during the Battle of Uhud in 625 CE, he sustained a severe eye injury from an arrow; according to tradition, his eye was miraculously restored by the Prophet Muhammad, an event that cemented his status and devotion. Beyond the battlefield, Qatada served as a scribe and a reliable narrator of Hadith, contributing to the corpus of sayings and actions attributed to Muhammad, which later became foundational for Islamic jurisprudence and theological understanding. His direct access to the Prophet made his narrations particularly valued by subsequent generations of scholars.
